output: I would like to ask my colleagues from UFAL, the Institute of Formal Applied Linguistics, Faculty of Mathematics and Physics, Charles University in Prague, I don't know if it needs to be mentioned
, but I would like to invite Ondřej Dušek, Rudolf Rosa, and Tomáš Musil, who have agreed to mentor, to come up
here with me to the stage and present how they can help.
I think,
who do we have on Zoom?
Ondra,
let's ask Ondra. Hello,
I’m Ondřej from MatFyz (Faculty of Mathematics and Physics), as Tomáš said,
I am a research assistant there and
I focus on natural language processing
, primarily chatbots, i.e., dialogue with computers, and language generation.
So, I can help with suggesting a machine learning approach for these things, or with some tools, and so on.
That's about it for me.
I’m
Rudolf,
I'm also
a computational linguist from MatFyz, so it
’s partly similar, some text processing, linguistic analysis of text, text generation, utilizing some tools we have, for example,
we have many APIs for these things, so essentially such things.
Hello, I’m Tomáš, and at UFAL
I mainly work on representation of meaning and
I can help with machine learning, whether it concerns text or image processing. Perfect.
So, I thank our colleagues, mentors, for introducing themselves, whether on Zoom or here.
I would like to ask the gentlemen to move to the chairs now, because we now have a workshop lasting approximately 31
minutes until 12 o'clock, during which we will be talking with Rudolf, Tomáš,
I will also invite David Košťák, a dramaturge from Švandova Theatre, and Martina Kinska, also from Švandova Theatre, a dramaturge, if they would like to take their seats.
It will start in a few minutes. In thirty seconds, the workshop before the detailed introduction of challenges will begin on Zoom, no longer in the form of a public stream, so
if you are wondering where to learn more about the challenges and where to discuss them,
it will be on Zoom,
go to our Slack channel Roboton.
If you don’t know how to access Slack, there’s a button with a link on roboton.cz that will take you there. And at 12 o'clock after the workshop on the topic of Theatre,
which is a project where artificial intelligence writes a play together with people, a detailed description of the challenges will follow. So
now I invite you all to participate in our discussion, where
I will be interviewing Rudolf Rosa, Tomáš Musil, both from the Institute of Formal Applied Linguistics at the Faculty of Mathematics and Physics of Charles University,
our guest will be David Košťák, and Martina Kinska from Švandova Theatre,
and we will be talking about the project of a theatrical play which helps a person write with the help of artificial intelligence, and the premiere of
this play will be in about a month, on February 26, here at Švandova Theatre, from where we are broadcasting Roboton. So
let’s get started.
I will sit down for a moment to
discuss the project. I will just briefly say
something as an introduction.
The project arose as a consequence... The frustration that not many celebrate the centennial anniversary of the word “robot,” which appeared on January 25, 1921, during the premiere of R.U.R.
at the National Theatre
– there was another premiere, an illegal one, underground, in Hradec Králové,
so it actually appeared even earlier.
Over the decades, thanks to Rudolf and his colleagues from the Švandova Theatre, Daniel Hrbek, to whom I brought it, they didn't dismiss it as utter nonsense,
that artificial intelligence could attempt to write a theatrical play.
And that team subsequently grew to include colleagues from DAMU,
submitted an application to the Technology Agency of the Czech Republic, within the ETA program, and succeeded.
So this whole initiative, a two-year project, is also supported by the Technology Agency of the Czech Republic as applied research in the social sciences.
It’s relatively unique globally. There have been attempts to have artificial intelligence write film scripts, short stories, fairy tales, poems.
And before I hand the floor over to my colleagues, perhaps we could conduct a small Turing test
for you, hackers and viewers watching this streaming.
If you agree with this, Rudolf,
you have
prepared an introduction, and
I will have to release it on my machine next to me. And I ask you to perhaps tell us what it is about.
It is, specifically, Karel Čapek’s R.U.R., which
I will read briefly.
The first robot says,
“Sir, machines cannot work;
we cannot reproduce robots.”
The second robot says, “We have multiplied work;
we have nowhere to put what we have produced.”
Alquist says, “For whom?”
The second robot, “For future generations.”
The first robot, “But we cannot manufacture robots;
machines only produce bloody chunks of meat.” “Skin doesn’t cling to meat, and meat to bones.
Shapeless clumps rain down from the machines.” And
the second robot says, “Humans knew the secret of life; tell us their secret.” And
this was written by Karel Čapek in EduWare, and you did
what with it?
Well, we took the tool we will be talking about today,
which automatically generates play scripts.
We entered this as input;
if you are familiar, it is the GPT-2 language model.
And then the tool continued in that text, that is, it generated a continuation.
And now we have a challenge for you, where you will see two possible continuations,
one is the original from the actual play R.U.R., and
the other was generated by our tool,
and your task will be to identify what came from a human
and what was automatically generated by artificial intelligence.
So just the instructions:
write us your tips. What you see on the left will be L,
and what you see on the right will be P, so give us
your estimates in Slack, there is a questions and answers channel,
you can also write within that channel if you think... Now we
are asking
what the machine
generated.
So let us know what you think, which version was generated by the machine.
If it is the one on the left, that is L, write L to Slack on questions and challenges. And
if you think the machine generated the right part of the dialogue, write P.
Shall we wait or shall we chat for a while? I have to
chat for a while,
so read, guess, vote.
So, how did it come about, Rudolf?
You began here with this trick, the Turing test,
in such a dramatic way, as one does in theater for a mathematician.
There are, of course, many difficult problems, but we were
already surprised from the beginning that today’s large language models – we use GPT-2 from OpenAI – can generate quite good text
on their own. If one wants to generate in English,
the basis is to take the model, prepare an input, which we saw,
and with a little luck,
the model will pick it up, recognize the format,
and continue in a similar way,
generating character names
, lines,
staying within the theme,
so the beginning is simple.
Now I’d like to ask David perhaps, who represents here the dramatic element
as a dramaturg of the Švandova Theater in Prague.
Please, what did you say when Daniel or who came up with the idea of putting on a play, whose text and dialogues would be written by artificial intelligence?
First of all, as a dramatist, I thought I was born in the wrong time,
that soon I’d be replaced by someone else,
but at the same time, it seemed important to be part of this project, because a rather interesting tool for authors has
emerged from it, not just theatrical ones; I know primarily computer games, actually, which are generated
independently, and the possibility of having some artificially generated dialogue in them is great.
But I don’t hide the fact that I approach this with curiosity and healthy skepticism.
And Tomáši, what feelings did you experience when it came, I don’t know, perhaps Rudolf, with this idea,
and you said, "I want this, it's interesting,"
or you said "WTF"? Well, definitely
I thought it was interesting and that it should be tried
and that I was curious how far we could get with it.
If I read about this
, in a more layman’s terms, everyone agrees, all the world’s capacities, that artificial intelligence, even though it’s called intelligence, isn't intelligent at all,
doesn't understand anything.
And how can a series of
ones and zeros, which have no reason to offer a testimony about the world, but merely listen to a person who presses a button and they do something,
how can they say anything substantial about human life? Well,
that’s quite a complex question.
I think... one thing is what we’ve already discussed regarding the presentation of those challenges,
namely, the boundary of what is or isn’t intelligent is constantly shifting.
It’s exactly as you said,
that is, we consider some behavior to be intelligent, then we replicate it by machine; that was,
for example, playing chess, which was for a long time considered something very intellectually

demanding, then it turned out that it can be machine-executed relatively easily, with significant computing power, but which, from today's perspective, isn't even that significant. Nevertheless, it can be machine-executed relatively easily,
and since then it hasn't been considered proof of intelligence.
As for whether the machine can say something substantial, I really don’t know.
To a certain extent, it’s always some kind of copying of something that has been put into the machine.
On the other hand, something interesting can also be created by copying and rearranging different pieces.
The question is, are people intelligent?
Many people say that a person simply absorbs what they have already seen
and recombines it, then releases it again. So,
we must not be excessively self-important about this.
If I may, I would also like to “steal” the FAZ quiz question.
I think we can learn quite a bit about ourselves from what the robot writes,
because what’s interesting is that it’s free from emotions, so it’s quite an analytical tool.
And, based on the dialogues and scripts the computer read,
I assume that what it then offered me was based on statistics of what most frequently appears in those scripts,
and from this perspective, the findings are quite interesting.
For instance, no matter which two characters meet, they often have sexual intercourse in the initial phases, before the probability changed
, no matter which two characters meet, so everything seems to be heading
not towards love, as literary scholars tell us, but towards that encounter itself.
It's interesting that the neural network is based solely on what you feed it;
if you feed it dramatic moments, exceptional in human life, then pearls immediately fall, but
on the other hand,
the times demand it. Extreme, dramatic situations attract our attention.
I would just perhaps return to the Turing test adapted for theatrical dialogue.
Have you seen those two... those two columns?
Which
of them,
I don't know, now we can see them again
; I ask Rudolph to reveal whether the computer generated the left or the right. Yes
, I can reveal it;
I don't
see it properly. So, the computer generated the column on
the left,
if I'm looking correctly.
You see it well. If necessary, it is necessary to go to the monitor.
But it is seen that even the author of the slide is not entirely confident in that distinction at first glance,
but the computer did generate that column, those dialogues that are on the left.
Let's look at the log, or I ask my colleagues if they are on the log, to... to check how many of you guessed correctly.
But these Turing tests show that it is much more complex to identify whether the machine is behind it or whether
the person did it themselves, perhaps with a simpler machine or tool.
So, maybe the question for all of us is whether the future lies in machines helping in theater, machines as scenery or lighting or some device that releases smoke,
I don’t know, I remember the theater from childhood, when people still went to theaters.
But perhaps, in the future, one of those tools that can push the theater forward will be artificial intelligence, or will it not be?
How do you see it, David?
Well, that's a question.
I think those possibilities exist,
but I believe one thing prevents them, and it's not technological;
it’s the ego of those authors and artists, the need to feel that we are the original ones.
And frankly, I can't imagine anyone openly admitting that someone else helped them with the writing.
But I think, or at
least for me, as I observed that program, the strength of what the computer generates lies in its randomness,
because often an author burdened by a certain probability and realistic games rarely dares to disrupt a logic that
the computer offers quite interesting sparks in this regard.
So I can imagine that if I were suffering from an author's crisis, I would generate a portion of the dialogue that could inspire me for further creation.
But I don't know if I’s confess to it.
At the same time, it seems to me that it gives the author the opportunity to take a step back and say that the game
is a bit silly, it's not my fault,
it was generated by artificial intelligence, so it wants to tell us something,
and we don’t understand it,
that’s our fault. The person sheds responsibility
. But I think it's incredible how it could help in the future in quantitative writing.
In the sense that when games are created today that self-generate, the possibility that they could be accompanied by dialogue that is itself generated is great.
I would like to ask all of you who are now following our little workshop, debate,
to ask questions, please do so via Slack, Robotono 2021,
there’s a channel, I think, questions
and sayings or questions
, so release your questions
and we will look at them in five minutes and try to answer some questions that come from those of you who follow and listen.
I would like to immediately build on what was said, that actually what a person puts into the network at the beginning as the input influences what comes out,
as shown in the tendency of artificial intelligence to immediately introduce sexual intercourse during the first minutes of the dramatic presentation.
I read a large, relatively large, article in MIT Technology Review yesterday, for 2021, the topic that should be addressed in the field of artificial intelligence
is precisely bias, as it’s called, that loading that led to the unsuccessful attempt in Britain with school applications when artificial intelligence evaluates, I don’t know, loans, etc.,
it may again contain some kind of injustice coded in thanks to the inputs.
How do you personally see the possibility of regulating, monitoring, or potentially? Should people even try to correct it
or give it a completely free rein
and not worry that the artificial intelligence itself is burdened by those inputs?
It is necessary to understand how artificial intelligence functions.
It has nothing available other than the inputs that we people give,
so it learns from what somewhere ar
ose. Typically, these are data that people create or provide
; it's not that artificial intelligence learns its own biases but rather that
it copies biases that people have long held.
So, it isn’t inherently bad.
It's good, and
it's so good that it copies our intelligent aspects, including our errors.
This is what's happening,
and, of course, there’s a lot of research on how to make it better than people
– to make it as intelligent as people but without those negative biases.
Tomáš probably knows a little something about this as well.
I believe we should definitely try to correct these problems, but
the question is how to do it technologically, because the most advanced methods, which are currently neural networks, are largely difficult to interpret.
We don’t know exactly how a neural network represents the data it receives.
And if we’re making decisions about people, and a particular group of people is systematically discriminated against at this moment,
that’s a pattern,
and that pattern is, of course, transferred into the network.
If the network sees in the data that this group of people doesn't get into schools, it will assign them a lower probability,
without exploring whether the reason they don't get in is due to a factual circumstance or a bias.
That isn’t reflected in the data.
How to eliminate this is a complex question.
Because, among other things, it’s not as simple as just saying, "I won
't include those elements that cause biases."
All data is ultimately corre
lated in some way. Research shows that even when, for example, resumes are automatically analy
zed, and data about a person’s race is obviously
removed, that information can still be extracted from the neural networks;
the information gets in, even if it's not explicitly written there.
How to prevent it from being there at all is a difficult research problem.
Perhaps a hackathon will yield a hack that contributes to removing biases from artificial intelligence—from us, imperfect organic clusters, flesh and bone,
or as Chuchvalec described when looking
at a person from the inside, in contrast to the beauty of machines.
So it’s one of the topics.
Before we move on to questions, I’d like to ask David—
because
Daniel says he will start testing only on Mondays—how things are progressing,
since he’s already seen the scenario and the actors are in place.
How will they learn lines that weren’t written by a living author but by a buzzing, glowing, blinking author?
I think it will be harder for them to learn, because the prompts aren't always entirely logical in
the dialogue. And the second thing specific to dialogues generated by a computer is that the robot is a bit like a child
or, in a sense, like an autistic person, because it doesn't account for the possibility that what is said isn't true.
So, within the framework of interpreting this text, we will need to incorporate that intrigue, so that it is interesting for the actors,
so that it can be justified why they are saying something,
because often the most interesting thing about theater is that something is said and something else is meant.
That will probably be our biggest interpretive task.
I’m now looking to see if we have any questions,
but I don’t see any.
Correct me if
we do have a question.
We don’t see any, so please do ask.
You still have 9 minutes
to ask the team behind the theater.
That team is quite broad, but includes representatives from
mathematics, psycholinguistics, or whatever they were recently called in the Guardian, psycholinguists from
Asimov and playwrights, like... I’m going to
ask about something related to the creation process and its transfer to the theater.
The whole play – and I take it to be a title, some notes, roles, and the structure of the scenes –
is entirely written by artificial intelligence? What is the share of
the human, the playwright, the dramaturg in the final performance we will see on February 26th, in a month here at the Švandova Theater? If I were to quantify it, I would say that
the human's share probably does not exceed about 10%,
but it's like this, that even the dramaturg’s share, when a live author is writing, is such, because the dramaturg gives some impulses.
Quite specifically, the play consists of several situations, dialogues and the input was practically only one short stage note introduc
ing the basic setup of the situation, those characters and the first two lines of that dialogue,
and the rest was generated by the computer, with us occasionally striking things out or
rejecting where the dialogue was heading, and it would start generating further.
That's quite standard guidance from a dramaturg to writing a play.
The only area where we have the greatest influence is that, of course, it is currently in a software stage where it doesn’t, or I haven't yet discovered that it can, construct larger opportunities.
So, the overall scenario is depend
ent on how we strung together those generated situations,
but that is a completely standard method of collage, montage,
which also happens with an author's text,
so we treat it like an author who is compliant and listens to us when we reject something.
This was basically an idea we had at the beginning, that there had been various texts that had been created with a share of artificial intelligence, where that share was here 10%, there 25%,
and we thought, that's not interesting anymore, so
let’s really give artificial intelligence as much say as possible,
and we agreed that those interventions would be minimal
and are essentially at the level of, as David said, what a person would intervene with in a text by a human author.
It’s true that it generates individual scenes independently of each other
; GPT generates text linearly. However, the project continues, and for this year, we plan to improve this by
implementing hierarchical generation, which would first generate a summary of the entire game,
and then this would expand into individual scenes, so that the intelligence also has some decision-making power over the structure of the game.
We’ll see how it turns out.
If you have a question, please write.
This is your last opportunity to ask on Slack, because otherwise, we have the final five minutes
and precisely five minutes from now the Q&A block on individual topics will begin, where we will also be discussing artificial creative intelligence with Rudolf.
But if you’re interested in the Theatre project, which will have its premiere at the Švandova Theatre on February 26th –
that’s in one month at 7 p.m. – there will again be a stream from Švandák on theatre.com. Everyone is invited to watch it;
it will be a worldwide premiere.
To our knowledge, nowhere else has a full-length theatrical play in a standard format like this yet been
created. It will be a play followed by a discussion with my colleague,
and I believe it will be a unique opportunity to assess where machine creativity with minimal human collaboration stands today
and whether it can produce an entertaining, dramatic, and engaging evening. Well,
since we don’t have any questions, I would like to thank our guests David, Rudolf, and Tomáš for spending half an hour discussing artificial intelligence in dramatic creation.
And I would ask the technical crew to play a teaser that will entice all of you to the premiere on February 26th.
